item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy.

🔍 Overview

KV-aware routing is designed for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. It addresses limitations in the previously introduced prefix-aware routing, which infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone. Because prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request, it cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Consequently, if an instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. Additionally, in multi-turn chats, each turn adds to the history; while a request is shorter than the configured PrefixLength, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns.

🧩 How it works

A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. KV-aware routing operates through three main components:

  • Model Container Reporting: The model container reports what it has cached.
  • Managed Cache Index: SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint.
  • Endpoint Routing: The endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. If instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A.

The endpoint picks among candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

⚙️ Key details

You turn on KV-aware routing in two places:

  • Add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents.
  • Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration.

Specifically, when you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. You do not configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing.

💡 Why it matters

This strategy ensures that requests sharing a prompt are routed to instances where that prompt is already in the GPU memory cache, maximizing computational efficiency. By tracking actual cache eviction and storage events rather than relying on static prefix hashes, the system prevents routing requests to instances where the cache has been cleared due to memory pressure.

#AmazonSageMaker #LLM #KVCache #Routing #Inference

Source: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution
item.description:
Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution

Recent technical updates in artificial intelligence focus on improving how agents manage long-term memory, evolve their internal states, and handle stale data or corrupted inputs. These developments span architectural innovations for memory storage, learnable policies for memory transformation, governance strategies for conflicting facts, and the impact of data corruption on recall accuracy.

🔍 Overview of Memory Innovations

  • KV-LTM: A new memory tier stores raw session text plus the KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering queries by restoring cached sessions.
  • EvoDisco: Formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery, allowing agents to learn which operators to apply rather than following a static schedule.
  • RegimeCouncil: An online router that arbitrates between local and global memory sharing scopes to manage stale facts without retraining the LLM.
  • Corrupted Memory Testing: A study testing whether intentionally corrupting training data prevents LLM agents from overfitting to recent events.

🧩 How It Works

KV-LTM Architecture This approach is complementary to retrieval and indexing. It treats text as the memory of record while using the cache as a recompute-free prefill accelerator. The design includes:

  • Storage records and budget-derived retention.
  • An append-only read path and bounded aggregation.
  • Analytical sizing where per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes for pinned BF16 full-attention and latent-cached MLA configurations.
  • A per-user-year storage estimate of approximately 0.34-3.6 TB at a 30K-token/day scenario, compared to approximately 49 MB of raw text.

EvoDisco Policy A learnable policy conditions on current memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate one of four semantic operators:

Operator Function
Abstract Compress related memories
Refine Decompose overloaded entries
Bridge Connect weakly linked experiences
Reframe Reorganize retrieved reasoning chains

The policy updates via a bi-level fitness: an inner signal scores transformation quality, while an outer signal scores strategic efficacy over past decisions.

RegimeCouncil Governance This system addresses the “memory conflict governance” problem where stored facts go stale. It uses a paired-evidence router with three modules:

  • Local Advisor: Tracks the latest outcome on a queried fact alone.
  • Global Advisor: Pools recent outcomes across all stored facts.
  • Meta Governor: Defaults to the Local Advisor to avoid cross-fact interference but switches to the Global Advisor when global pooling shows a positive utility margin.

⚙️ Key Details and Results

  • KV-LTM Evaluation: Requires no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation. It uses per-session prefill to emulate valid cache reuse. System-level comparisons on LongMemEval indicate that commercial assistants often score below models reading history offline, consistent with content loss between write and read phases.
  • EvoDisco Performance: In a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench, EvoDisco outperforms strong memory baselines like MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are observed on ALFWorld, with improvements of +8.8 to +12.9 points over MemP and +16.4 to +17.9 points over MemRL.
  • RegimeCouncil Performance: Across LongMemEval update streams and historical drift tests on TempLAMA and TAQA, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes. Ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
  • Dream Hypothesis Test: An agent using Claude Opus 5.5 stored learned information in text memory and rewrote it nightly from transcripts with 5-40% corruption. The results showed that corruption did not help the agent apply earlier learned tasks. Replacing details in 40% of turns lowered recall from 76% to 60%. Random-text corruption had no consistent effect because the model recognized it as corrupted and excluded it from memory.

💡 Why It Matters

These updates address critical inefficiencies in long-term AI interactions. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, solving the problem where personal assistants accumulate months of conversations but struggle with derivation and selection. EvoDisco moves beyond fixed memory operators, allowing agents to dynamically decide how to transform their memory based on strategic efficacy. RegimeCouncil provides a lightweight method to handle delayed feedback from stale facts without the complexity of full LLM retraining. Finally, the corruption testing suggests that pretrained models can easily separate corrupted text from real events, implying that fair tests of memory evolution require learners that cannot make this distinction as easily, such as those fine-tuned on specific corrupted data or operating in invented worlds.

#AIMemory #LLMAgents #KVCache #AIResearch #LongTermMemory

Source: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants Source: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory Source: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents Source: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory

item.title: FlashOffloading Boosts LLM Serving Throughput by Offloading KV Cache to Host DRAM
item.description:
FlashOffloading Boosts LLM Serving Throughput by Offloading KV Cache to Host DRAM

FlashOffloading is a new host‑DRAM‑centric inference architecture that fully offloads the key‑value (KV) cache in large language model (LLM) serving, delivering higher throughput while meeting a 30 ms time‑per‑output‑token (TPOT) service‑level objective.

🔍 Overview

  • In LLM serving systems the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, quickly exhausting high‑bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity and limiting concurrency.
  • Moving the KV cache to host DRAM frees HBM space and allows higher concurrency, but the added cache management and host‑to‑device (H2D) load overhead increase inference latency, so the concurrency gain does not translate into effective throughput.

🧩 How it works

  • Rolling HBM cache for prefill – keeps a small active portion of the KV cache in HBM during the prefill phase.
  • Hot cache for decode – stores frequently accessed KV entries in host DRAM for decode.
  • Reverse sparse index – provides zero‑extra miss‑lookup overhead when locating KV entries.
  • Compute‑load overlapped kernel – overlaps computation with H2D data movement to reduce offloading latency across the entire pipeline.

⚙️ Performance gains

  • Deployed with GLM‑5.2 using multi‑token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill‑decode disaggregated platform.
  • Prefill throughput improves by up to 1.38×.
  • Decode throughput improves by up to 1.91×.
  • Gains are achieved while staying within a 30 ms TPOT constraint.

🚀 Availability

  • FlashOffloading has been integrated into an open‑source serving framework. See the implementation at this https URL.

#LLM #Inference #KVCache #DRAM

Source: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving

item.title: RecSA Enables Million-Token Context Lengths with Logarithmic Selection Cost
item.description:
RecSA Enables Million-Token Context Lengths with Logarithmic Selection Cost

A new development in context length extrapolation, Recursive Sparse Attention (RecSA), has been introduced to address the scaling limitations of dense attention. While dense attention becomes prohibitively expensive at lengths near 1 million tokens, RecSA provides a method for efficient prefill and decoding by reducing selection costs to logarithmic complexity.

🔍 Overview

Existing sparse attention methods often rely on selection costs that scale linearly ($O(L)$) with context length. RecSA overcomes this by building a tree structure over the KV cache. In this architecture, each node in the tree summarizes its subtree using a single key and one mean-pooled value. This allows each query to achieve $O(\log L)$ selection cost and read only $O(\log L)$ entries.

🧩 How it works

RecSA utilizes a hierarchical selection mechanism that maintains performance even at extreme scales. Key components of the architecture include:

  • KV Cache Tree: A tree structure where each level above the tokens selects a maximum of $k$ candidates.
  • Shared Poolers: One pooler per layer, shared by all levels, is distilled from dense attention to generate keys for summary nodes.
  • Logarithmic Softmax: Summaries of unselected candidates share a single softmax with the exact tokens, ensuring comprehensive attention coverage.
  • Positional Encoding: Using Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), each entry’s position is defined as its index among candidates at its specific level. This ensures relative distances remain within the range observed during training.

⚙️ Key details

RecSA was evaluated using a model initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62 billion tokens at a 32K training length. Performance results demonstrate significant improvements over standard sparse and dense baselines:

Metric RecSA Performance Baseline (Dense + DCA)
RULER Score (1M tokens) 60.5 40.0
Prefill Speedup (524K) 3.2x -
Decoding Speedup (524K) 3.8x -

Tested on a single H200 GPU, optimized kernels for RecSA were found to be faster than dense attention for both end-to-end prefill and decoding tasks across context lengths ranging from 64K to 2M tokens.

💡 Why it matters

This approach addresses a critical bottleneck in large language model deployment: the scarcity of long-document training data and the quadratic cost of dense attention. By keeping relative distances within training bounds and reducing the memory and compute overhead of KV cache selection, RecSA allows models trained on shorter sequences to extrapolate effectively to contexts as large as 2 million tokens.

#RecSA #LLM #MachineLearning #KVcache

Source: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time Source: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer Source: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost Source: SPARE: Fast Linear Attention Decoding with Compact Recurrent States Source: SKIM: Pruning Large Language Model Agents via Selective Knowledge Informed Masking Source: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction

item.title: Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents
item.description:
Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents

Multi‑turn agentic workloads accumulate context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. Each new turn resends the full conversation history – system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses – causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly.

🔍 Overview

  • In Prefill‑decode (P‑D) disaggregation, a prefill node builds the key‑value (KV) cache for the prompt, while a decode node retrieves those KV blocks to generate the response.
  • Conventional disaggregated serving moves KV cache only from prefill → decode. This one‑directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi‑turn workloads:
    1. After a response, the decode node holds KV entries for both the prompt and newly generated tokens. The prefill node cannot retrieve these entries for the next turn and must recompute KV projections for the previous response tokens.
    2. Session state is kept on the decode node but not on prefill nodes, increasing the chance of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill side.
  • When a full cache miss occurs, the prefill node recomputes KV projections for the entire conversation history, consuming more accelerator capacity and increasing time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT).

#AIInference #KVCache #MultiTurnAgents #AWS

Source: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Encoder‑Only Healing Enables Parameter‑Efficient KV‑Cache Compression
item.description:
Encoder‑Only Healing Enables Parameter‑Efficient KV‑Cache Compression

A new study shows that fine‑tuning only the encoder after post‑hoc SVD‑based KV‑cache compression matches full‑factor healing while using far fewer trainable parameters and optimizer memory.

🔍 Overview

  • The paper Freeze the Decoder, Heal the Encoder (submitted 25 Sep 2026) investigates parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning recipes for KV‑cache compression.
  • It reveals that comparing recipes with a shared learning rate can create a misleading advantage for smaller‑parameter arms.
  • By assigning individual learning rates to each factor, the apparent win of encoder‑only healing disappears, exposing true parity.

🧩 How It Works

  1. Low‑rank cache conversion – An already‑pretrained model’s key/value weights are factorized into:
    • a down‑projection (encoder) and
    • an up‑projection (decoder) forming a low‑rank, multi‑head‑latent‑attention‑style cache.
  2. Healing fine‑tune – A short fine‑tune (“healing”) is applied to recover accuracy lost to truncation.
  3. Learning‑rate strategy – Instead of a single shared rate, each factor receives its own tuned learning rate.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Shared learning rate bias: When arms differ in trainable‑parameter count, a common learning rate depresses larger arms’ means and inflates variance, fabricating a multi‑seed‑significant advantage for the smallest arm.
  • Encoder‑only healing parity: With per‑arm learning‑rate tuning, healing only the encoder achieves the same accuracy as healing the decoder or both factors.
  • Resource savings:
    • 3× fewer trainable parameters
    • 3× less optimizer‑state memory
  • Empirical verification:
    • Tested on the vision‑language model Qwen2.5‑VL‑3B‑Instruct with three random seeds per configuration.
    • Replicated on a text‑only testbed across two backbones.
  • Practical recipe: Encoder‑only healing is a lower‑memory drop‑in method for retrofitting low‑rank KV‑cache compression during training.

🚀 Why It Matters

  • Provides a memory‑efficient path to enable low‑rank KV‑cache compression without sacrificing model performance.
  • Highlights the importance of per‑arm learning‑rate tuning when comparing fine‑tuning strategies that differ in parameter count, a caution applicable beyond this specific setting.

💡 Takeaway

For practitioners seeking to compress KV caches, applying a short healing phase to the encoder alone—while tuning its learning rate separately—delivers parity with full‑factor approaches at a fraction of the memory cost.

#KVCache #ParameterEfficient #ModelCompression #FineTuning

Source: Freeze the Decoder, Heal the Encoder: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for SVD-Based KV-Cache Compression Source: Lossy Compressive Text Autoencoders Source: Sparse Attention Is Matrix Approximation, Not Choosing from a Bag of Values Source: SFT-as-Context Mitigates Forgetting in Supervised Fine-Tuning Source: REMORY: Learning Residual Memory for Context Compaction

item.title: KVFetch adds temporal recall channel to improve KV‑cache compression
item.description:
KVFetch adds temporal recall channel to improve KV‑cache compression

KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression was submitted on 23 Sep 2026. It introduces a new mechanism to address a key limitation of current KV‑cache compressors used during long‑context LLM inference.

🔍 Overview

  • As context windows grow to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, KV‑cache compression becomes essential for efficient inference.
  • Existing compressors belong to three families: score‑based eviction, summary compensation, and offload‑and‑recall.
  • All three decide what to keep or recall solely by content relevance to the current query.

⚙️ Problem with existing KV‑cache compressors

  • A cache supports two access modes: associative lookup by content and sequential traversal by position.
  • Current compressors implement only the associative (content‑based) mode.
  • This omission matters for tasks such as retrieval‑augmented generation, code completion, and structured‑data extraction, which need verbatim reproduction of identifiers, field values, or code tokens.
  • Under compression, content‑based eviction keeps the head of a sequence but discards its continuation, causing “sequential forgetting” – a failure that persists despite better scoring, larger budgets, summary compensation, or dynamic re‑scoring.
  • Sequential forgetting is identified as the dominant source of remaining quality loss under compression.

🛠️ KVFetch design

  • KVFetch is a training‑free, drop‑in framework that adds a temporal recall channel to any score‑based compressor.
  • It demotes evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier.
  • It detects active copying through a monotone read pointer.
  • It prefetches positional successors into fixed‑size hot‑tier slots without increasing attention cost.

📊 Results

  • Evaluation on RULER‑16K under an iso‑budget control shows:
    • Verbatim copying recovery improves from 0.8 % to 78.4 %.
    • The 13‑task average score rises by +8.4 points, with gains concentrated on tasks requiring sequential access.
  • On LongBench, where no task requires sequential access, the temporal channel stays dormant and imposes no cost.

🚀 Availability

  • KVFetch is presented as a drop‑in framework, implying it can be incorporated into existing score‑based compressors without additional training.
  • The work is hosted on arXiv Labs, a platform that encourages community collaboration and upholds values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy.

The story is based on the arXiv preprint titled “KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression.”

#KVCache #LLMInference #Compression

Source: KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression Source: Task-Oriented Key-Layer KV Communication for Efficient Latent Multi-Agent Collaboration Source: Algorithmic Scratchpads and Curriculum Staging for Arithmetic Reasoning in Tiny Transformers Source: SPIN: Shadow Predictive Indexer for Sparse Attention Source: A Self-Pruning Transformer: Extreme KV-Cache Compression with Universal Attention Source: LRCC: Generalizing Low-Rank Compression with Conditional Computation Source: OnlineQAT: On-Policy Distillation for Ultra-Low-Bit Large Language Models

item.title: AttSVD Enables Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression
item.description:
AttSVD Enables Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression

AttSVD is a new, interpretable low‑rank compression method that adapts to each prompt’s attention geometry, reducing key‑value (KV) cache memory while preserving performance.

🔍 Overview

  • KV caches of autoregressive transformers grow linearly with context length and dominate memory at long context.
  • Traditional training‑free remedies evict low‑importance tokens, an irreversible choice along the sequence axis.
  • AttSVD keeps every token but stores it more cheaply along the feature axis.

🧩 How it works

  • Performs an online, per‑prompt truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) that retains only the directions attention actually reads.
  • The retained rank determines the proportion of persistent per‑head KV memory that is kept.
  • Two decode‑time caching strategies are offered:
    • Accumulating – suited for short generation regimes.
    • Streaming – suited for long generation regimes.

⚙️ Key details

  • Per‑matrix energy rule: sizes the logit space and the attention mass independently.
  • Attention‑aware basis: truncates only in the spaces attention reads, preserving both attention logits and output.
  • Provides free, per‑head interpretability insights into effective rank and the geometry attention consumes.

📊 Performance

  • Across multiple models, on an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite, AttSVD stays on par with the dense cache while using up to 50 % of the KV‑cache memory.

#KVCache #LowRank #Transformer #MemoryEfficiency

Source: AttSVD:Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Attention-Guided SVD Source: Mask-Guided KV Cache Eviction in Block Diffusion Language Models Source: WavePrune: One period is often enough for RoPE Source: Recurrent Looped Transformer Source: Monte Carlo Estimation for KV Cache Eviction Source: Readout Stability in Prefill-Only Decision Models:Zero-Label Prediction and Inference-Time Compute Allocation

item.title: Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits
item.description:
Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits

KV‑cache reuse can cut inference cost in retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) and agentic systems, but edits to retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state can make cached contexts stale.

🔍 Overview

  • Under causal self‑attention, a local edit can affect downstream KV states.
  • A full re‑prefill restores consistency but is costly.
  • Refreshing only the edited span can leave downstream dependencies stale.

⚙️ Budgeted Repair Approach

  • The problem is framed as in‑place repair = budgeted recomputation.
  • Training‑free position‑selection policies are evaluated on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits.

📊 Findings

  • Across three model families, all policies fix direct‑edit cases; derived cases separate the policies.
  • With the primary budget, a contiguous edit‑local window recovers ≥ 0.94 of the post‑edit answer margin and outperforms attention‑based, KV‑deviation, and structural selectors.
  • Mechanistic analysis: position sets that work under clean‑state transplantation can fail under actual recomputation because scattered positions inherit surrounding staleness.
  • The edit‑local advantage depends on adjacency and largely disappears when the answer‑bearing text moves downstream.
  • Answer‑relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior; failure severity is difficult to predict.
  • Repair using the edit‑local window is 13–21× faster than a full re‑prefill.

💡 Implications

  • When the dependent text remains adjacent to the edit, unconditional edit‑local repair provides a fast, cost‑effective solution to stale KV caches.

#KVCache #RAG #ModelRepair #AIInference

Source: Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits Source: Long-Context Demonstration Selection Using State Space Models

item.title: K/V-Cache Interventions for Persona Control in Llama-3.1-8B
item.description:
K/V-Cache Interventions for Persona Control in Llama-3.1-8B

Researchers have studied K/V-cache interventions as a structured surface for persona control in decoder-only language models, specifically by transplanting a target-conditioned K/V trajectory into a source-persona generation.

🧩 How it works

This method is characterized as trajectory-level transplantation rather than isolated persona-representation injection because the transplanted trajectory carries the target’s own generated token history. To test this, a same-token-sequence control was used to decode an identical token sequence under source versus target conditioning, which reproduced the sign and layer localization of the L28 representational shift, suggesting the shift is not explained solely by imported token history.

⚙️ Key details

Testing involved 13 intervention configurations applied to Llama-3.1-8B for a fixed source-to-target persona pair. The results showed a dissociation between representation-level alignment and behavioral expression:

Layer-Band Replacement V-gap (Alignment) Behavioral Result
Early 0.91 Strong local V-space alignment
Mid (Layers 9-20) 0.89 Combines target-marker expression with preserved lexical diversity
Late 0.84 Strong local V-space alignment
Full 0.94 Comparable alignment to mid-layer but different lexical-diversity profile (TTR 0.65)

Additional findings include:

  • Lexical Diversity: Mid-layer replacement produced a TTR of 0.77, compared to 0.65 for full-layer replacement.
  • Position Perturbations: Both lag and shuffle operations uniformly suppressed target-persona expression, representing a common behavioral failure.

💡 Why it matters

These findings indicate that representation-level similarity metrics alone are not sufficient predictors of downstream persona expression. The K/V cache serves as a controllable but structurally constrained intervention surface. Note that these results characterize representation-behavior dissociation in a high-signal setting and do not establish universality across all models or persona pairs.

#LLM #KV-cache #Llama-3.1 #PersonaControl #MachineLearning

Source: K/V-Cache Interventions Dissociate Representation Alignment from Persona Expression in Decoder-Only Language Models

item.title: New InertiaKV Methods Boost Decoding-Time KV Cache Efficiency
item.description:
New InertiaKV Methods Boost Decoding-Time KV Cache Efficiency

A paper submitted on 3 Sep 2026 to the Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence category introduces aggressive KV‑cache eviction techniques that rely on temporal aggregation rather than solely on scoring function improvements.

🔍 Overview

  • Decoding‑time KV cache compression has traditionally emphasized better token scoring functions.
  • The authors highlight that the temporal rule aggregating scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail.
  • Their experiments show that exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) aggregation preserves ranking order and makes many scorer modifications indistinguishable at the eviction‑set level.

🧩 How it works

  • EMA‑based aggregation couples layer weighting and temporal retention, providing stability for value‑norm and entropy variants, which stay highly correlated with attention and keep retention sets nearly unchanged.
  • Scorers such as KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and cause substantial degradation.

⚙️ Key details

Method Core idea Reported impact
InertiaKV EMA‑based decoding‑time eviction Improves decode throughput compared to full‑refresh baselines
InertiaKV‑Lazy Periodic‑refresh variant of InertiaKV Yields 1.34–1.46× decode throughput relative to full‑refresh InertiaKV
Score‑Free decoding Scores the full context once at the first decode step, then freezes the ranking Average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring
  • Experiments span six open‑weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench‑v2, and RULER benchmarks.
  • Results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors, without claiming scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper provides code, data, and media associated with the article for reproducibility.
  • Links to the PDF and supplementary material are available through the arXiv entry.

💡 Why it matters

  • By focusing on temporal aggregation, the proposed methods achieve higher throughput without sacrificing generation quality.
  • The findings suggest that stable aggregation can make many scorer variations effectively equivalent, guiding future KV‑cache compression research toward aggregation strategies.

#AI #KVCache #Decoding #TemporalAggregation

Source: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation

item.title: Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency
item.description:
Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency

New research introduces two distinct approaches to optimizing key-value (KV) cache memory usage in large language models to address bottlenecks in long-context inference and reasoning workloads.

🔍 Overview

KV cache growth poses a significant memory bottleneck for LLM serving. Two new frameworks, GrowPage and SGD-KV, provide methods to manage cache memory more efficiently.

🧩 How it works

Framework Methodology Primary Focus
GrowPage On-demand budgeting Dynamically adjusts KV capacity based on runtime demand variations.
SGD-KV Summarization-Guided Compression Uses a head-aware diagnostic task to prioritize attention heads.

⚙️ Key details

GrowPage

  • Treats KV capacity as a runtime resource that evolves during generation.
  • Maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to estimate demand.
  • Integrates with PagedAttention to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
  • Adjusts capacity by compressing states or acquiring additional physical pages as needed.

SGD-KV

  • Employs a chunk-summarization diagnostic task to identify heads specialized in hierarchical information aggregation.
  • Reduces KV cache memory usage by up to 75%.
  • Maintains performance on benchmarks up to 1M context tokens.
  • Tested on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3-32B models.

💡 Why it matters

Both methods offer improved performance-to-throughput or efficiency-to-accuracy trade-offs, enabling more effective long-context inference and reasoning.

#LLM #KVCache #AI #MachineLearning #Inference

Source: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving Source: SGD-KV: Summarization Guided KV Cache Compression

item.title: HeadWiseKV Compresses Key-Value Caches in Hybrid Language Models
item.description:
HeadWiseKV Compresses Key-Value Caches in Hybrid Language Models

In a new optimization development, researchers have introduced HeadWiseKV, a training-free framework designed to compress the residual global key-value (KV) caches of hybrid language models. During long-context inference, retaining a growing KV cache during decoding consumes substantial GPU memory and can reduce generation throughput. This bottleneck remains in hybrid language models because their residual global-attention layers can dominate context-dependent cache demand. HeadWiseKV addresses how to allocate this state under an aggregate KV-residency budget while preserving the models’ native local, recurrent, and linear paths.

🧩 How it works

HeadWiseKV optimizes KV cache allocation through several architectural mechanisms:

  • Predictable Cache Demand: The framework assigns each physical KV head a static, multilevel history window, making cache demand predictable before serving.
  • SeqCalib Algorithm: HeadWiseKV formulates the allocation as a restricted operational rate-distortion problem and uses SeqCalib as its core policy-generation algorithm. SeqCalib processes layers in execution order and conditions each decision on the lower-layer policy used at deployment, thereby accounting for interactions across depth.
  • Grouped-Cache Runtime: A grouped-cache runtime materializes the selected policy as actual per-head KV residency rather than a mask over a full cache.

📊 Key details

The framework has been evaluated for performance and downstream quality:

  • Model Evaluation: Quality was evaluated across four hybrid long-context models, and physical residency and serving behavior were studied on Qwen3.6-27B.
  • Quality Preservation: HeadWiseKV retains near-Full-KV RULER and LoCoMo quality across the evaluated models.
  • Memory Efficiency: In a fixed-model systems study, the framework reduces sampled peak device memory by 8.59% at a 112K context length.
  • Context Extension: HeadWiseKV extends the largest verified successful context from 114K to 161K.
